utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Turning to defence, do you hear us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Blaskic, do you hear. THE DEFENDANT (in interpretation): I am sorry, I did not have translation for that, which channel? JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): I am not sure -- I did not hear the answer from General Blaskic. Did you hear everything as the interpreter -- did the interpreters hear that on the other side? Is everything heard? Did you hear General Blaskic? We can just be sure one more time about that. General Blaskic, turning your microphone on, would you please say that you heard me? This is just to be sure that the interpretation booth is hearing you, to interpret what you have to say, should the Trial Chamber want to hear what you have to say. THE DEFENDANT (in interpretation): I hear you very well, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Good, thank you very much. You may be seated. Do my colleagues hear me? Mr Li, do you hear? First, I would like to know who is representing the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr President, Judge Riad and Judge Li. My make is Mark Harmon and appearing with me and representing the prosecutor's office as well to my left is Mr William Fenrick and to my right is Mr Andrew Cayley, and Mr Gregory Kehoe. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. Turning to the defence, are both of the law firms being represented here? I do believe they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are, your Honour. Russell Hayman representing the accused, with my colleague, Anto Nobilo. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. The Trial Chamber will sit as long as needed in order to hear the arguments over four preliminary motions which have been submitted by the defence for General Tihomir Blaskic. Nonetheless, the four motions which have been presented have to do with two which were filed on 4th December 1996 and two which date from 16th December. They deal with the failure to punish, mens rea, international armed conflict and the vagueness of the form of the indictment. These should be part of the rules, subject to Rule 73 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which cover them. In the meantime, the Trial Chamber has also been asked by the defence to review an application in order to issue a subpoena to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina demanding the production of evidence which would be exculpatory. The application dates it from 28th February. The Trial Chamber, unless there is an objection from the prosecutor, or the defence, suggest that first we would hear the explanations presented by the defence, and then the response of the prosecutor having to do with that application. That is the application which, I make clear, deals with a request for an order from the Trial Chamber for a production of a certain number of -- a certain amount of evidence from Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that, the Trial Chamber will consult both the prosecutor and the defence in order to find out what order should be followed in dealing with the preliminary motions. I will first give the floor immediately to the defence so that he may argue for his application, asking the Trial Chamber to order Bosnia and Herzegovina to produce a certain number of exculpatory materials. I would like to explain something first. I say that first we would deal with the question, first of all, because it is somewhat out of the context of the preliminary motions, as they were supposed to be argued today, and tomorrow, and also because there is a connection both with a motion which was settled by this Trial Chamber, having to do with the forced production of evidence which has been asked by the defence of the prosecutor, and this application which was settled on 27th January, as I just said, and also because the request from the defence may also have an analogous relationship with the requests, or rather two requests, which were formulated by the Office of the Prosecutor with Trial Chamber 2 presided over by Judge McDonald, asking for a forced production of evidence from the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This dispute that was presented to Trial Chamber 2 is now being reviewed, and this is why I believe that, before we take up the preliminary motions, this Trial Chamber must hear both parties in respect of this request. After that, we will deal with the preliminary motions themselves. Mr Hayman, I give you the floor, in order to expound on your application of 28th February on the request for forced production of evidence that you were asking from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I give you the floor, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Several weeks ago, the defence learned that the prosecution had submitted, I believe initially, under seal and in camera, applications for subpoena duces tecum to both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those applications were submitted in this case, that is they bore the number of this case, the title of this case, and they pertained to this case; that is, the subject matter of those subpoenas pertained to this case. We were not given notice of those filings. We were not served with the papers. We were not even given notice of the fact of an ex parte in camera filing in the case. When we learned of these subpoenas, we made a decision to file the instant application to which your Honour has referred, and the reason is we believe that, whatever the subpoena powers of this Tribunal are with respect to non-party nation states, that that power must be available to both parties on an equal basis, and an equal footing, and we believe that follows not only from fundamental notions of international customary law, but from Article 21 of the Tribunal's Statute, section 4(e), which provides that the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality, (e) referring to the ability to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses, on his behalf, under the same conditions as witnesses against him. Although a subpoena duces tecum seeks documents, it is in effect a subpoena to a witness. It seeks to compel a witness, a custodian of record, to appear and produce documentary material. So we believe that Article 21, section 4(e), clearly requires that this power, this service of process, or rather access to the process and power of the court in order to bring witnesses and relevant evidence to the attention of this Tribunal, must be available to both parties on an equal footing. We, therefore, filed our application seeking the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum to the appropriate authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina for certain evidence, which we believe is clearly exculpatory. We believe (1) it exists and (2) that it is clearly and will be clearly exculpatory, with respect to our client. We are in a position to seek the subpoena now, because we have asked the prosecutor for this material, and it has not been produced, and we therefore have reason to believe he does not possess this material; rather it remains in the possession of the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I should note that, of the two subpoenas issued on January 15 of this year, on behalf of the prosecutor, rather for the prosecutor and as a result of her application, one of them is still in full force and effect. The other, although it has been suspended, has not been withdrawn, and is still in that sense in existence. For reasons pertaining to the constitution and the internal politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we would request that this subpoena be directed to the President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr Alija Izetbegovic, and I would ask -- JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Now what order are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to the subpoena duces tecum that we seek, your Honour. It has to go to an individual, I would submit. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): This is a request that you sent to the Trial Chamber on 15th January; is that correct? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I am saying that, with respect to the -- the 15th January is when the two subpoenas issued were sought by the prosecution. We filed our application for a subpoena and, with respect to that subpoena, I wanted to add that -- I have consulted with my colleague, and we believe that the proper party to whom that subpoena would be addressed would be Mr Izetbegovic, and Mr Nobilo can elaborate on that. Also we have identified one additional category of records that we think would be highly relevant and highly exculpatory, and I can either read those into the record at a suitable point, or we can file those in writing at any time. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Nobilo, do you want to add anything, or shall I conclude, Mr Hayman, that you have completed with your presentation? MR NOBILO (in interpretation): Yes, your Honour. I should just like to explain our extension of the request for the subpoena to be addressed to Mr Alija Izetbegovic, the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Actually heading Bosnia-Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state, and member of the UN, is a three member Presidency. Alija Izetbegovic, he is the President of that Presidency. However, as all state functions and the state structure after that date has still not become operational in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency does not have full control over the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, therefore, I feel it would be important to address the subpoena to the person who actually has power over the people who have command of these documents, which we consider to be exculpatory, and Alija Izetbegovic is without doubt the number 1 authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all the documents we are requesting are in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, in a country that is not fully functional along democratic lines, nor is power being wielded as stipulated by the constitution, we feel it is important that the subpoena be addressed to the person who actually has power and who has the possibility to get hold of those documents, and that is why we extend our request to the subpoena being addressed to Mr Alija Izetbegovic. That is all, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Prosecutor, would you care to respond to the entire application of 28th February? If we have understood in it, there is an additional request, or at least another authority, in this case the President of the Presidency, that is Mr Izetbegovic. I give you the floor, Mr Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. In respect of subpoena duces tecum application by the defendant in this case, your Honour, the prosecutor's position is that the Tribunal can issue subpoena duces tecum to Government and Government officials. We have taken that position in the two subpoenas that are now presently being heard by Judge McDonald. Our view is that, if these instruments to secure evidence are available to the prosecutor, they should be equally available to the defendant in this case. Our view also is that the only limitation on issuing those subpoenas is a finding by the court, or the Trial Chamber, or the judge of the Tribunal that these requested items are relevant. I wish to inform the court more fully of the status of the two subpoenas that are presently before Judge McDonald. One of the subpoenas that was issued to Croatia and to Mr Gojko Susak, the Minister of Defence, or his representative, has been temporarily suspended on the understanding that there would be a request for assistance from the Croatian Government, that there would be discussions, and that there would be production of documents, and obviously it is still an on-going process, but the prosecutor is able to file a report with Judge McDonald if there is not meaningful compliance with a request for assistance, and we are reserving our judgment on that at the moment. In respect of the subpoena issued to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the subpoena was directed to, first of all, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and, secondly, to Mr Jelavic, who is the custodian of the records of the HVO archives. We have had approximately five hearings on that subpoena duces tecum application. The next hearing that is scheduled will be scheduled for 16th April 1997, at 10.00 am, when Judge McDonald has requested oral argument on three issues, and she has invited the parties to submit their briefs in respect of those issues she has identified. The three issues that she has asked for briefings are the power of a judge to subpoena a state, the power of a Tribunal judge to subpoena a Government official, and the remedies that are available to her for non-compliance. The briefing schedule that has been established on that by Judge McDonald is that briefs are due to be filed by the 1st April 1997. Reply briefs are to be filed by 11th April 1997, and then the hearing itself, oral argument will occur on 16th April 1997. Secondly, in respect of the subpoena to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to Mr Jelavic, Judge McDonald has set a hearing for the 18th April 1997, at 10.00 am, and has directed Mr Jelavic to personally appear before her in order to show cause why he should not be held in contempt to comply with numerous court orders that she has issued in respect of that particular subpoena. Your Honour, in the course of complying with the court's order for discovery, we have been in the process of undergoing a rigorous examination for documents that are responsive to the court's order, that are exculpatory, and, while we have not yet furnished to the defence all of the documents that he has requested, we continue to search for those documents, continue to make production as we acquire them, and will continue to do so in the future. That is all I have to say, your Honour. Thank you very much. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Before we move to the preliminary exceptions, I have a number of comments I would like to make. The first is really a question which I wanted to ask both parties: do you consider that this dispute is a follow-up to the previous order of 27th January, the order of 27th January, which, as I recall, permitted the Trial Chamber to settle, because I thought that it would be definitively settled, that is having to do with the production of evidence? This is the first question. In other words, the request which Mr Hayman presented, is this part of a subsequent disagreement having to do with this decision of the Trial Chamber of 27th January, or is the application new? The second question is to know whether the Trial Chamber hearing the Blaskic case, which I have the honour of presiding, does it have jurisdiction over becoming part of the investigation, if you like, and become a sort of an investigating magistrate ordering this or that state to supply this or that piece of evidence? Is this not up to the prosecutor? The prosecutor is responsible for the investigation. Is he not the one who is supposed to do as he does in many other cases which are being presented to the International Criminal Tribunal, when he builds up his investigating dossier? In other words, I would like to summarise my position: does this Trial Chamber, does it have the jurisdiction to put itself into the service of one of the parties -- today it is the prosecutor, tomorrow it is the defence -- in order to help constructing the file of the prosecutor? Tomorrow will be for the file of the defence, and then the next day, we will get another request from the prosecutor, another request, and I am speaking of Trial Chamber 1. I am not talking about the one which is presided over my colleague, Judge McDonald, but this Trial Chamber, which will hear the Blaskic case, does it have the legal jurisdiction in order to serve one or other of the two parties? Or are we now settling a dispute which is a kind of consequence of the previous decision, which was part of our decision of 27th January? This is a very significant question, because what I see behind the request -- I now turn to Mr Hayman particularly -- is, of course, either try to wait, or to have us wait so that the theoretical questions which Judge McDonald asked on 18th April -- this is all of this rather sensitive issue of knowing at what point the trial can really begin. There are ways of putting things off. So these are questions I would like to ask both of the defence. Recalling that the defence initially said that the prosecutor did not supply the exculpatory material, when I hear this, I rather believe that we are now talking about a dispute which derives from a poor application -- I am using that word "poor" in inverted commas -- having to do with the decision of 27th January, at that point I believe that the Trial Chamber does have jurisdiction in order to settle an issue having to do with any kind of a decision taken. Or, on the other hand, does Mr Hayman ask the Trial Chamber the way the prosecutor asked Mrs McDonald, not really with an understanding whether he is moving to the other Trial Chamber, because this one is involved in something else. I would like to know whether this Trial Chamber has jurisdiction legally. I make another observation, and I say also that Mrs McDonald also asked herself that question, because she considered that she had to ask different sub-questions, which would not be dealt with before the middle of April, 16th or 17th April. So I believe that the parties now must confront their responsibilities. I first turn to Mr Hayman so that he can try to clarify the discussion, having to do with this request, which, in fact, does come from the defence, and after that I will give the floor to the prosecution. I give you the floor, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The defence submits that the Trial Chamber has jurisdiction in either case over this matter, and over our request. In other words -- JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Are you talking about the Tribunal or the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber. The present chamber has jurisdiction, whether this is an outgrowth of our discovery motion from last year, or whether it is a new application, and allow me, if you would, for me to elaborate. First, I do think our application is related to our discovery motion of last year, because, in that motion, we sought much, if not all of the same material we are seeking in this subpoena. We sought it from the prosecution. We had a good faith belief that they would have collected this information in the course of their investigation. Having obtained the order of this court earlier this year, compelling the prosecution to look through their files for the exculpatory evidence that we set forth in great detail in our motion, having had an initial production from them of material that did not include the material that we seek, largely records of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we then concluded that it was appropriate for us to seek a subpoena duces tecum compelling the appropriate authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina to produce those records. Had we not first determined that the prosecution did not have these records, I think we, the defence, would have been open to the accusation, whether well-founded or not, that we were seeking to circumvent the Rules of Discovery by seeking from a third party, by subpoena, what the prosecution possessed, and either was or was not obligated to provide to us under the Rules of Discovery. So I think there is a close nexus or connection between our discovery motion and our application for a subpoena duces tecum. However, we also would submit that this Trial Chamber has jurisdiction over our application, even had it been a new matter unrelated to prior proceedings before this chamber. Under Rule 54 of the Tribunal, that Rule states that, at the request of either party, or proprio motu, a judge or a Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants or transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of an investigation, or for the preparation, or conduct, of the trial. Now, if the Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber's jurisdiction was limited to issuing orders, or subpoenas, for purposes of the actual conduct of the trial, then Rule 54 would not include investigations and the preparation phase. I submit we are in the preparation phase. We are close to trial itself, and clearly Rule 54 confers jurisdiction on this Trial Chamber to hear and judge and decide our application for a subpoena duces tecum. I also submit that it is sufficient and it will reserve judicial resources, at least in one event, for this Trial Chamber to decide this issue in that this Trial Chamber has already heard the arguments of the parties concerning the relevance and exculpatory nature as we argue of the very materials we seek. You are familiar with these items. Your Honours are, and it is an efficient use of the Tribunal's resources for you to consider this application. Lastly, would it be appropriate -- I sensed in the colloquy with the court, the underlying question whether it might be appropriate to wait for the larger issues being considered by Judge McDonald to be resolved prior to ruling on the defence's application. Until and unless the other subpoenas that have been issued -- that were issued on the application of the prosecution, until and unless they are withdrawn, and have no legal effect, the defence submits it would be inappropriate for the prosecution to have subpoenas in effect served on parties with, in fact, as I understand it, a hearing on calendar on 18th of this month for an order to show cause why a witness should not be held in contempt of this Tribunal for failure to produce these materials. It would be inappropriate for this type of process to be available and to be utilised with the vigour and force that the Office of the Prosecutor is, in fact, utilising those subpoenas, and for the defence to have to sit and wait for a month, approximately a month, for a hearing to occur, before another Trial Chamber, and we do not know, of course, whether there will be a ruling at that hearing, whether the matter will be concluded on 16th April, or whether there will be some further life. So not only, we submit, would it be unfair for us to have to wait, but we think time is of the essence. The trial is very close in this matter, we expect. It may take some period of weeks to obtain the documents that we seek by subpoena. It may take some period to evaluate and examine them, and time is a very, very dear resource to the defence. We need to obtain these documents to prepare for trial, and we hope to do so without any further delay. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. Turning to the prosecutor, on these three points, I summarise and say that the Trial Chamber, that is the request as part of our decision of 27th January. Number 2, even if this were not a consequence of the 27th January's hearing, the conflict -- this must be brought to our attention pursuant to 54, and we should not wait for the theoretical requests which came from Mrs McDonald. In order to give the floor to you, I would like to say first there is an initial question would I like to ask: do you think that the request of the defence is a consequence of an application which has been judged by the defence to be imperfect with respect to our decision of 27th January, where we stated that, should the application not be properly conducted, the affair would be settled, and that the Trial Chamber, as I said, would take any consequences of a legal nature from this that would be coming up. So the question is do you believe that Mr Hayman's request is part of this dispute, having to do with the 27th January's decision? Then, the following question: Mr Hayman says to us that the Trial Chamber 1, in any case, would be competent, and the second question I would like to ask is why, Mr Prosecutor, did you refer the matter to Mrs McDonald's chamber one month ago in order to ask for the production of certain evidence, and why did you not refer the matter to this Trial Chamber? Third point, if we have to wait for the answers to the questions which my colleague, Judge McDonald, asked, who was the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber 2, do you consider yourself that this is essential for the solution of this question? I give you the floor, prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of your first question, whether this is related to a dispute on discovery and your decision of 27th January, I think in part it is related to the decision of 27th January. It is not that we have a dispute at this point. It is that the prosecutor, in responding to the court's order of 27th January, has been obligated to review an excess of half a million pages of material, and we have embarked on that endeavour in good faith. We continue to do so on a daily basis. We continue to try to identify materials from that excess of a half a million pages, and collect it, and produce it to the defence. We, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, are in an on-going process, and I think that we are coming close to the end of that process, however. We have made productions, and we will continue to make productions as quickly as we are able to do so. In respect of your second question, your Honour, whether the Trial Chamber would be competent, our view is the Trial Chamber would be competent to issue a subpoena duces tecum, and we agree with the defence that Rule 54, among other rules and articles of the Statute, give this Trial Chamber the authority to do so. Your third question, your Honour, is a question of why the prosecutor's office did not refer the issue of the subpoena duces tecum to the Trial Chamber and instead referred it to Judge McDonald. In my view, your Honour, the prosecutor's office could have referred it to either, the confirming judge or the Trial Chamber. I thought personally, your Honour, and I made the decision to refer it to Judge McDonald, because in an enquiry by this Trial Chamber as to the relevancy of certain items contained in the subpoena duces tecum, it was my view that I could get into a discussion with this Trial Chamber and with members of the Trial Chamber that would lead me to a position that I could not ethically defend, and that was that I would be engaged in ex parte communications with the Trial Chamber about evidence that I have or may need, and, in my view, your Honour, I considered that the more prudent and safe course would be to go before the confirming judge. Those are the answers to the questions I have, your Honour. I believe you may have had a fourth question. I did not note it down, but those are the answers. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): The fourth question stems from your previous comment, because I always thought that, when you referred the matter to Mrs McDonald's chamber, this was not to pollute this one which is dealing with the case. I thought that, if you made that choice, it was because Mrs McDonald's chamber would have to sort through all of the different elements that were there, and that it would have been better for it to be a judge who was not the judge in the trial who would go through that sifting process. So this comes out of your last argument. But you say that you were afraid of getting into an ex parte procedure. Are you not afraid that, if this Trial Chamber, over which I preside, responds favourably to Mr Hayman, that, if one were to imagine the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina responding favourably to the order I would give, we in this Trial Chamber, my colleagues and myself, would have an enormous mass of papers, and might have to decide, as Mrs McDonald is having to do, to make decisions over relevance or irrelevance of certain documents. Is this Trial Chamber in a position, or authorised to make this kind of -- to do this kind of a sifting/sorting process, with the judge becoming involved with one of the two parties, which is why I thought that your ex parte idea was what had guided your choice. But the last point I would like to add is that we, in fact, have now come into total confusion, and unfortunately, I am sorry that the members of this Trial Chamber were not consulted. Had I received your request, Mr Harmon, we would have done something else, because things have become very confused now. With this Trial Chamber, if it were to respond favourably to the request, we are going to have documents, the same ones. Some are going to come to Mrs McDonald, who will sift through them, but she has an objective position. Other documents will come to this Trial Chamber. I will then not sift through them. I cannot, I am not in a position to sift through them. If I did, I could be blamed for doing so by the prosecutor, and if I do not, then I just do -- then I act like a letter-box. That is all. So I think that the interpretation of Rule 54 means that any judge can order any state to do something, but we are always trying to ensure a fair trial, but I am not settling the issue. I am simply saying that this is an issue which is far from having been settled, and I am not at all surprised that Judge McDonald felt it necessary to ask a whole series of previous questions, and I do not know what we are going to do, I will speak about it with my colleagues. This is the question that I wanted to bring out. Do you have any comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour, the issues that I identified when I made my selection certainly apply to this Trial Chamber as well. Rule 54 does not identify any particular judge or any particular Trial Chamber that is necessary to hear this application. So perhaps, your Honour, any application such as this, that is present, could be heard by a different Trial Chamber in order to avoid the possibility of the polluting the neutrality of this chamber. So those would be my observations. Your fourth question, however, comes back to mind, your Honour, and your fourth question was whether or not these legal questions that are before Judge McDonald should be -- what impact that has on this application. Certainly, in terms of efficiency of this court, in terms of legal efficiency, Judge McDonald has a briefing schedule and has identified very significant issues, which she has yet to decide. I only point out that, if this court were to issue a subpoena duces tecum at this time, and Judge McDonald were to decide to the negative as to each of her first two questions, we would have an anomalous result where, this chamber has made a finding that a subpoena duces tecum can be issued, and a judge of the Trial Chamber would have come to a different conclusion, and the subpoena which we have submitted before Judge McDonald could possibly be resubmitted before this Trial Chamber as well. So I think from an efficiency point of view, it may be best to defer the application until a decision has been made before Judge McDonald. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Yes, Mr Hayman. You realise what the question is. You raised this question before this chamber. You are right from the theoretical point of view. It is the very basis of the functioning of this Tribunal. The judge, like the prosecutor, can order the production of certain documents. But it depends on which judge, the permanent judge, the confirming judge, or the trial judge, and you are here before the trial judge. I am simply saying that either we will say that we can do it, and suppose that Judge McDonald says that she cannot do it, or vice versa. In any event, we have to place ourselves in the position of the States. The States do not know of chamber 1, chaired by Judge Jorda, or chamber 2 chaired by Judge McDonald. They only know of the International Tribunal, and here we have a real problem, and, before closing this debate, it is up to the Chamber to rule on it, of course. I would like to ask you whether you insist on your application, whether you are going to modify it, simply to hear your comments regarding the position of the defence, and afterwards of the prosecution. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I did want to comment that the court has expressed a concern that it may be called upon to sift through a voluminous records and engage in conduct that may be somehow inconsistent with being the Trial Chamber in this case. My understanding of how this process would work, your Honour, is that the documents, once a subpoena is issued, would be produced, and they would be simply given over to the party on whose behalf the subpoena was issued. The court would not undertake a review of the documents in the sense that an investigating judge or magistrate would, but rather the documents would come to the party that subpoenaed them and then, from those documents, whatever may be relevant and appropriate to produce at trial would then be produced at trial and in that way the Trial Chamber would become acquainted with and familiar with the material in the course of trial. With respect to timing and the -- JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Let me comment on your first observation. If the Chamber of Madam McDonald should be engaged in a conflict -- we must speak very clearly. We cannot do just anything. If one chamber of this Tribunal, or the prosecutor, or you, are engaged in a conflict with a state, a dispute with a state, it is a procedural dispute. It is annoying, but that is our life as Judges. But even if this chamber does not examine those documents, does not review them, this is not a theoretical hypothesis. The authority, or the state in question, does not wish to deliver these documents, and then we engage in a process of forcing that state to do it. Is that chamber going to preserve the serenity required for trying this case in one sense or another regarding General Blaskic? It is not a question of individual qualities or characteristics. That is not the point. Just suppose that one of the states which needs to supply the prosecutor's file does not prove to be efficient and the Security Council, or somebody else, may force it to, so this chamber too would have to intervene, and I am again asking the prosecution and the defence would that be normal. If you, as the defence, and you, as the prosecution, consider this to be normal, I would like you to say so, so that we take note of something that I would not like to happen. If we embark upon this road, yes, the Chamber is competent. It will ask a state, in this case Bosnia, to supply a certain number of documents. Yes, the Chamber will have a mandate to force or to issue a condemnation against that state. We can do that. If you answer, "Yes, you can do that, and your impartiality will not be called in question", I would like you to say that to me, quite officially, so that this can be taken note of in the minutes. What I would not like is that, when the trial proceeds, after one, two, three months, one day General Blaskic, you, or the prosecution, might say "Yes, but you are not impartial, because you engaged in a dispute with such and such a state", and I think that this is clear now. I am sorry for taking a bit more time, and I would like to hear your comments for the last time, yours and of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where I come from, your Honours, it is entirely normal for the trial court to be involved in the compulsion of testimony in the process, particularly with the defence of issuing subpoenas. There is nothing abnormal about it in the laws and courts of my country, and I also do not believe that it is somehow inappropriate, nor in any way taints or pollutes this Trial Chamber to be part of the process by which the evidence that you will review that comes before you. Because the defence maintains this is a very important part of the tapestry of fabric that will be painted in this case. Will the evidence that comes before you, will it come from sources that have a responsibility and have some legal obligation by virtue of orders or subpoenas from this Tribunal or otherwise to produce relevant evidence, or will the evidence be produced by volunteers, and only by those who choose to come forward and perhaps accuse my client? Will the defence not have the power to bring before this court the records and files of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the court has a more complete, we would maintain, picture of the events relevant to this case? So even if we engaged with a different Trial Chamber, this process of trying to obtain evidence, trying to compel the production of evidence before this court, those very facts, that very process, in other words, the defence maintains, is relevant, to your consideration of the evidence and the lack, perhaps, of certain types of evidence that ultimately appears before you. So we do not believe it is a taint, nor in any way inappropriate for this Trial Chamber to be involved in the compulsion of evidence and the process by which evidence comes before you. We think it is appropriate, it is useful, it is necessary, and ultimately, when the case is tried, we will be discussing those issues with the court. I agree with your Honour that there is a state of some element of confusion created by the fact that this issue, the underlying issue of the subpoena power with regards to non-party nation states, is before two trial chambers at one time. First, I want to assure the court that I came -- we came, the defence came to this Trial Chamber with our application, because we felt that was most appropriate, and there is nothing in the Rules of this Tribunal, or in the Statute, suggesting that we, the defence, should go anywhere else. I am not taking issue with Mr Harmon's decision to go to another Trial Chamber. That was his choice. But I do want to impress upon the court, we came here because we believed this is where we should be. We are in your court, and, of course, if you want to send us somewhere else on this matter, that is certainly your power, your discretion, and your right, but I do believe it was appropriate for us to come before you in the first instance. That being the case, I still believe there is a danger that, if the defence's request languishes and is put on hold, while the prosecution is still in a position to attempt to aggressively compel the production of inculpatory evidence, what if they get their evidence, their subpoenas are complied with, and then a month, six weeks, or two months from now, Judge McDonald, or perhaps the appellate chamber decides there is no such subpoena power over a non-party nation state, and yet this evidence has been produced pursuant to their request for a subpoena, the inculpatory evidence is here. The exculpatory evidence is not, because our subpoena languished. I would submit, if that is allowed to pass, the accused would have to be set free. He could not receive a fair trial. He would have been denied equal access to the powers of the Tribunal with respect to obtaining witnesses and evidence, and I do not want that to happen. I think that would be wrong, it would be inappropriate, and some remedy needs to be fashioned, without delay, so that either our subpoena, the one we seek, is issued, or the prosecution subpoenas are stayed and rendered a nullity until these larger questions are resolved. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Yes, Mr Prosecutor, I give you the floor. At the end you said what I feared, Mr Hayman. You reassured the President of this chamber, but in the last few metres you did not reassure him, because you put your finger on the questions that I am worried about most, and that is a contradiction between the decisions of the two chambers, and, if we address ourselves to the same chamber, there is less chance of a contradiction, and basically you said that, if before Madam McDonald's chamber, one cannot pre-judge, but if the prosecution does obtain a certain amount of evidence, and in this chamber, let us assume that we do not obtain the same results, then you would be the first to say so, and that was what I feared when I said a moment ago, do not come and tell me later here is the first result. You would come immediately before the Chamber and say, "He must be released". That was what I feared, and I think I was right in fearing it. I give the floor now to the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to point out a couple of items to the court. In the first place, I believe that the Trial Chamber would be, and could be, put in a position where it would be more than essentially a postbox, conveying documents that were produced pursuant to the subpoena duces tecum. It could occur that, in respect of some of these documents that have been sought, that a privilege, issue of privilege, could be raised, and the issue of privilege, this Trial Chamber would have to examine the documents and make decisions relating to the contents of those particular documents. So I would just like to point that out in particular. In respect of Mr Hayman's point, that the subpoenas have requested inculpatory evidence, clearly we have requested a number of items, but, in our request to both countries, we have requested items which would be exculpatory, as well, and information that would be exculpatory to General Blaskic. I might add, your Honour, that, in terms of assuaging the fears, at least at this point, our efforts to acquire documents from the parties has resulted in approximately twelve pages, perhaps sixteen pages of documents being produced to the prosecutor's office, many of which were exculpatory, and many of which have been turned over to the defence. So my view is, your Honour, that, as I said before, a concern that I have is certainly an anomalous result between contrary decisions being reached by this chamber and by Judge McDonald. However, I do support the Tribunal's position to issue subpoenas. That has been our position. We are on record in stating that Judges have the right and Trial Chambers have the right to issue subpoena duces tecums to governments and government officials and we will be advocating that position before Judge McDonald on April 16th. I have nothing further. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Therefore you agree, like Mr Hayman, that this chamber is competent to issue this kind of order, this kind of subpoena? You are agreed, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am agreed, your Honour. I am not saying that it is the only chamber that could issue this kind of an order. I think any Trial Chamber could issue an order, and I think any judge could issue an order as well. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Fine, thank you. I think we have explored the totality of this issue, and, if you would be kind enough, let us pass on to the preliminary motions, and I shall try to put some order in the debate now. We have four preliminary motions on which the parties need to present arguments. We have the choice between two possible orders: a chronological order. Two preliminary motions were issued on 4th December, on failure to punish and charges alleging command responsibility, and two others regarding existence of international conflict, and defects in form. There is a great deal of documentation that has been submitted to these trials. We feel that these motions could be grouped according to their nature. Some of those motions have to do with incompetence, Article 113(e) of our rules. Some others are motions of defects in form regarding the indictment against Mr Blaskic, and two other motions are mixed. They contain at the same time elements of incompetence, and elements of defects in form. Therefore, after our discussion, we propose we proceed in the following manner: we start from competence in the direction of defect in form. We are first going to treat the motion that is clearly a motion of competence regarding the criteria that the Chamber should adopt according to the defence, to define the international armed conflict. That is the first motion which we are going to argue. The second motion is a mixed one. It contains elements of competence and elements of defects in form, and it is the failure to punish. That will be the second one we are going to deal with. The third has to do with mens rea, but, as no text has been cited, we will treat it as third, and we will end with the general motion on all the complaints the defence has regarding the form of the indictment. Therefore, I repeat, after the break that we are going to have in a moment, we are going to first treat the question of an international armed conflict, then the failure to punish and, three, mens rea, and, four, the defects in form. The hearings will be heard this afternoon and for the whole day tomorrow. The Chamber would not like to be in session on Friday, in view of the numerous writings submitted to us. I hope you will be able to argue insisting on the principal points. Of course the Chamber will not prevent you in expressing yourself at length, but each one of you referred to your systems. In my system, the attorneys can be asked to clear up certain points in their written motions. Therefore, we are going to suspend the session until 4.00, and we will start at 4.00 with the first defence motion, having to do with the existence of an international armed conflict. (3.35 pm) (A short break) (4.10 pm) JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Hayman, you have the floor. No, I am sorry, we nearly forgot, we are going to have General Blaskic brought in. Perhaps he could take his headphones. Will you pick up your headphones. Can you hear me? Stand up, please. I should like to ask you, your conditions of detention are correct. THE DEFENDANT (in interpretation): Mr President, everything is fine, except the possibility of going out into the fresh air. By decision of the president of the detention centre, I am not allowed to walk, to have a walk outside in the fresh air ever since the 20th January. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): You know that it is up to the President you should address yourself, not the Chamber. I should just like you to tell us in public here whether the conditions are satisfactory. We heard you. You know whom you should address. THE DEFENDANT (in interpretation): Thank you, Mr President, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Turning, your Honours, to the defence motion to dismiss certain counts of the indictment for failure to adequately plead the existence of an international armed conflict, I would first note that certain counts of the amended indictment allege grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and that, to apply to this case, the acts in question must have been committed -- that is for Article 2 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions to apply to this case -- the acts in question must have been committed as part of an international armed conflict. The amended indictment alleges that there was an international armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the years in question, but that is all it says. It is a conclusory allegation, and the position of the defence is that that conclusory allegation is insufficient to state that element of the grave breaches offences, namely the element that there was and existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, with respect to the acts alleged, an international armed conflict. We argue in our motion that, to find the existence of an international armed conflict, such that Article 2 would apply, it is not sufficient simply that a conflict between two international parties existed somewhere on the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time in question, or even within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A conflict, for example, in the north-eastern corner of Bosnia and Herzegovina between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, for example, the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would not, we submit, convert any conflict between Bosnia and Herzegovina, between citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, into an international one. That is, the existence of an international conflict in one corner of the country would not turn a civil internal dispute between the citizens of the same country also into an international armed conflict. In fact, this view was that adopted in the appellate decision on jurisdiction in the Tadic case, which clearly stated in paragraph 72 of that opinion, that, to the extent that the conflicts had been limited to clashes between Bosnian Government forces and Bosnian Serb rebel forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had been internal, unless the direct involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could be proven. I am reading from paragraph 72 of that opinion. Notwithstanding the separate opinions with respect to that decision, the majority opinion stands for that proposition. Thus we submit to establish the existence of an international armed conflict, something more than the presence of a foreign army on the soil of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be alleged in the indictment, and, in fact, not even that is alleged. We simply have the conclusory allegation that there was an international armed conflict at the time. What is that something more that we submit must be alleged? Well, there are two authorities to which we turn for guidance that we submit should be referred to for guidance, and again, first, I refer to the Tadic appellate decision on jurisdiction in paragraph 76, where the appellate court held: "If the Security Council had categorised the conflict as exclusively international, it would follow that the International Tribunal would have to consider the conflict between Bosnian Serbs and the central authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina as international. Since it cannot be contended that the Bosnian Serbs constitute a state, arguably the classification referred to would be based on the implicit assumption that the Bosnian Serbs are acting not as a rebellious entity, but as organs or agents of another state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." The International Court of Justice addressed a similar issue in Nicaragua v the United States, and there the International Court found that the United States completely supported, organised and financed the Nicaraguan contras. Yet the court found that that level of involvement by the United States was insufficient to state the requisite identity of parties between the United States and the contras, such that the conflict between the contras and the Government of Nicaragua was transformed into an international one. Specifically in the Nicaraguan opinion the court held at paragraph 2.19 that the conflict between the contras forces and those of the Government of Nicaragua is an armed conflict which is not of an international character, governed by the law applicable to conflicts of that character, whereas the actions of the United States in and against Nicaragua fall under the legal rules relating to international conflicts. Here the indictment fails to allege we maintain an essential element necessary for the existence of an international armed conflict, namely that the Republic of Croatia exercised control, complete control, over the HVO forces. Without that allegation, those charges that are based on Article 2, grave breaches, should be stricken. Now, the main response of the prosecution to our motion is that we are trying to litigate the evidence in the case, and that this is an inappropriate time to litigate whether there is adequate evidence or not. We are not trying to litigate the evidence. We are challenging the adequacy of the pleading, that is of the amended indictment, and we submit that the amended indictment should contain an allegation on this critical element, and then, of course, if they plead it, they must prove it at trial, in order to sustain the charge. The danger in not having to plead it is they may not have to prove it, and they may also change what, in fact, the nature of the charge is. So the accused should have the benefit both of notice and of certainty with what he is charged, namely that, if the charge includes an allegation that there was an international armed conflict, and that grave breaches apply, it should be a specific allegation, it should state the requisite level of control over an outside force, over one of the actors with respect to the conflict in question, and, unless that is properly alleged, our position is those applicable counts of the amended indictment should be stricken. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you, Mr Hayman. The prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Mr President, your Honours, in answering this motion of the defence, the prosecution regards it fundamentally as an issue of pleading. The manner in which I intend to answer each of the arguments put forward by the defence in their motion is to use the same subheadings as they have done in the motion that they filed with the court, and include in that the prosecutor's own position, and also briefly address the reply of the defence to the prosecutor's response. The defence, first of all, state that Article 2 requires evidence of international armed conflict, and the prosecutor does not take issue with this proposition, but would rearticulate it in the following manner: an international armed conflict must be proven in order to establish subject matter jurisdiction over discrete acts which are alleged violations of Article 2, the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Conventions. The defence then state in their motion that the prosecutor has failed to sufficiently allege the existence of an international armed conflict. Now, that allegation is contained in clause 5.1 of the amended indictment, and reads as follows: "At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of international armed conflict and partial occupation existed on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What is the purpose of that allegation? In order to answer that question, one must ask the question what is the purpose of the indictment, of this instrument, and, in order to do that, we must look to the Statute, the Rules, and the existing jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Now, I will not go into this matter at length, because my learned friend, Mr Kehoe, will be addressing you on the sufficiency of the indictment as a whole, but I would read out to you Rule 47B, which is a derivation of Article 18.4, and that says the following: "The indictment shall set forth the name and particulars of the suspect, and a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime with which the suspect is charged." Looking to the existing case law of the Tribunal, what guidance can be gleaned from that? In the Prosecutor v Djukic, Justice McDonald stated on a motion on the indictment that the indictment has to give the accused warning of the nature of the crimes with which he is charged and set out the factual basis for the charges. Mr President, you yourself stated in the Prosecutor v Djukic that the obligation on the prosecutor is to state succinctly the facts and crimes with which the accused is charged, the name and particulars of the suspect must be contained in the indictment, the concise statement of facts, and the class of acts with which the accused is charged. The guidance that this gives us in respect of the allegation contained in 5.1 in my submission is that it must be a concise expression of the nature of the conflict that is required for the triggering of the grave breaches provisions. It must serve to warn the accused of the nature of the conflict in relation to these particular crimes. It must succinctly demonstrate to the accused the nature of the conflict in relation to these particular crimes, and it is the prosecutor's position that that is exactly what 5.1 does. Now, the defence in their motion argue that a memorandum on jurisdiction that was filed at the same time as the original indictment in this matter is filed in order to in some way prop up an inadequate indictment. Now, that memorandum on jurisdiction, which deals exclusively with international armed conflict, also has attached to it a statement of facts also exclusively dealing with the matter of international armed conflict and a large bundle of evidence. This is part of the supporting material that was filed with this indictment originally in November of 1995, and which Justice McDonald considered when she confirmed the indictment under Rule 47A. Now, the defence have this supporting material. It does contain all of the details regarding the allegation of an international armed conflict. To stress this point further, the indictment and the memorandum on jurisdiction are separate documents, but they must be read together. It is incorrect to state that that memorandum on jurisdiction in some way props up the indictment. That is not the position. It is a separate document, and it contains evidence, matters of evidence which should be addressed by this court at trial, not in a preliminary hearing such as this. The defence in their reply accept that factual issues as to whether or not an international armed conflict existed between the HVO and the BIH is a matter of evidence which must be decided at trial, and I quote from their reply: "The defence agrees that factual issues in this case must be resolved at trial. Whether or not a conflict between the HVO and the BIH constituted an international armed conflict is a factual issue that cannot be determined before trial." If we are to determine this issue now, then it begs the question as to why we should not determine other factual issues which are relevant to the grave breaches provisions, as to whether or not there has been, for example, wilful killing. That would clearly not be appropriate. The prosecutor's position is that the whole issue is fact sensitive. The question of whether or not this allegation is sufficient has been related by the defence as to whether or not there is an international armed conflict at all. It is not possible to answer that question at this stage, because no evidence has been heard by you. In the reply to the prosecutor's response, the defence argue that at a minimum, some sort of legal test should be set as to enable, when the facts are heard by the court, to place both parties in a position where they know what the legal position is as to the existence of an international armed conflict. It is the prosecutor's position that it is not possible to set such a legal test in a vacuum, absent of evidence, and I would very briefly refer the court to two decisions, the first being the Karadzic and Mladic case, and the Nikolic case, both cases, Mr President, in which you presided at Rule 61 proceedings. In both of those cases, you found in existence, as a provisional matter, an international armed conflict, but it was a fact based decision, relying on evidence submitted by the prosecutor in both oral and written form. The law and the fact in this area, that of international armed conflict, cannot be divorced. Since at this stage you cannot hear fact, now is not the appropriate time to set a test. That would be for you to do at trial. As I have stated, and I hope I have made clear, your Honours, I do not propose to address you on the fact of the law referred to by the defence. I would merely say, in summary, that the allegation as to the international armed conflict is adequate. Every indictment confirmed by this Tribunal contains a similar or identical allegation. That the allegation is sufficient is demonstrated by the defence's lengthy arguments on why they say an international armed conflict is not in existence. It is a mixed question of law and fact, and it is a matter for trial. That is the position of the prosecutor, Mr President. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Hayman, the Trial Chamber is now going to give you the floor to speak about the second preliminary motion, dealing with the insufficiencies or inadequate nature in the indictment, having to do with the failure to punish. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I, your Honour, have one minute to respond to Mr Cayley's comments on the first motion? JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He has cited a standard that the indictment must state as well as the crime "facts". There are no facts alleged with respect to the issue of international armed conflict. What are alleged are conclusions. Partial occupation, we do not know, partial occupation by whom? Partial occupation where? As to the actual armed conflict, we do not know who the international parties are that are allegedly in conflict with respect to that allegation, and it is not enough to say that facts are inextricably bound up with the law. This element should be pleaded with some factual specificity so that (1) there is notice and (2) the prosecution is bound to prove what they have alleged. The indictment should be a final accusatory pleading. It should not be a moving target, and that is the essence of our argument on that motion. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Since I have allowed a reply to be given, I can now give the floor back to the prosecutor. Would you like to respond to what was said? Would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will be very brief, Mr President. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Very brief, please, one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Less than a minute, Mr President. The only point that I make is this: the defence have been provided with a large bundle of evidence, and a memorandum on jurisdiction that identifies all of the points that the defence is complaining have been not adequately pleaded in the indictment. For us to, for example, change the parties to any alleged international armed conflict would be ludicrous, because we have provided evidence in which we identify those parties. That is just an example. But I stress this is a mixed question of fact and law. It cannot be decided at a preliminary hearing such as this. The defence, and they acknowledge that they have received this, have received a memorandum on jurisdiction explaining the legal position of the prosecutor, they have received a statement of facts outlining the evidential position, and a large bundle of evidence in support of that statement of facts. That is the position of the prosecutor, Mr President, thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): I would also like to point out to you that the Trial Chamber has not received this memorandum on the conflict. I can also indicate this to the Registry. Is that normal procedure, Mr Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am not hearing the translation, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): I had made an observation which dealt with the prosecution, because I had said that in any case they had not received any information, any memorandum about the armed conflict. During the deliberations we can go back to that. Mr Hayman, I give you back to the floor to speak about the second motion dealing with failure to punish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. No International Tribunal in history has based the criminal liability of a commander for acts of subordinates solely on the commander's failure to punish subordinates for wrongful acts. This Tribunal should not be the first in history to do so. Allow me a moment to state why the defence believes this is an issue of great importance. The amended indictment states in paragraph 5.7 that the accused bears criminal responsibility as a superior for the acts of his subordinates based solely on an alleged failure on his part to punish subordinates, having allegedly learned of the acts of subordinates after the fact, that is after the time of their commission. That follows from the use of the disjunctive, or in the last sentence of paragraph 5.7. Thus it provides that it is alleged there is independent liability for the failure to prevent wrongful acts of subordinates having learned that subordinates were about to commit such acts, in a totally separate offence for which liability as a principal is alleged for the alleged fact that the accused learned that subordinates had committed wrongful acts, and the accused allegedly failed to punish the perpetrators thereof. Now, in their response to our motion, the prosecution suggests that the defence is attempting to draw an artificial distinction, and that is their phrase, between failure to punish and failure to prevent at page 14 of their response. If they intend in the indictment to allege failure to punish only as a species of failure to prevent liability, the defence would withdraw its motion. We do not contest the fact that failure to punish, if an element of a charge of failure to prevent, could state an offence under international customary law, but, for that to be true, the failure to punish would have to have a causal relationship with the reoccurrence of a crime or a wrongful act, namely a wrongful act was committed by a subordinate, the commander learned of it, failed to punish the subordinate, and the subordinate committed an additional crime. That is, there is a reoccurrence of the crime. Within that context, we do not contest the legitimacy of failure to punish as a claim or an allegation, but, under international customary law, international convention law, failure to punish standing alone has no bona fides. It has never been a crime. No one has ever been charged or punished with it, we maintain, and it should not be a crime in this case before this Trial Chamber. So the discussion in the briefs with respect to whether international customary law supports criminal liability as a principal for a commander who fails to punish subordinates requires an examination of the case law, of convention law, and other sources, and I would like to briefly go through those sources, commencing with Additional Protocol 1 to the Geneva Convention, assuming for the moment that it applies to this case and to this accused. There are two sections of Additional Protocol 1 that have been discussed by the parties with respect to this motion, the first being Article 61, which appears in a number of places, but, for instance, on page 19 of the prosecutor's response. Article 61, section 2, bears on the issue of failure to prevent and failure to punish liability. There are three reasons the defence urges that Article 62, section 2, does not and cannot confer liability on a commander based solely on a failure to punish subordinates where the commander learns, after the fact, that misconduct, or a crime has been committed by a subordinate. First of all, the first clause, or phrase of Article 86, section 2 reads that a fact that a breach of the conventions or of this protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superior from penal or disciplinary responsibility. We maintain that penal or disciplinary responsibility is a matter of national law. That refers to disciplinary measures. It does not refer to principal liability, or liability as a principal for the underlying act having been committed. Article 86, section 2, continues: "If the superior knew, or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time that he [that is the subordinate] was committing or was going to commit such a breach", this is the second key phrase of Article 86, subsection 2, "was committing or was going to commit". By its very terms those phrases restrict themselves to failure to prevent liability. In other words, they refer to acts that either are on-going, and hence can be prevented if action is taken, or have not yet occurred, i.e. was going to commence. They do not refer to acts that have already been completed and hence, for that additional reason, Article 86, section 2, cannot be a basis for command responsibility or the liability of a commander based solely on a failure to punish subordinates. Then finally, continuing with this section: "And if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress the breach", "prevent or repress", what does that mean? "Prevent", we know what prevent means. It means prevent something from happening in the future. "Repress", I submit, has a similar meaning. It does not confer liability as a principal for failure to punish acts of subordinates when those acts are learned of after the fact. So, for three different reasons, Article 86, subsection 2, cannot and does not confer liability on a commander, based solely on the commander's failure to punish subordinates, where the commander learns after the fact of the wrongful acts. Perhaps I should have said this at the outset of my argument, that our motion is in the nature of a motion on jurisdiction. We are suggesting that Article 7, subsection 3, of the Tribunal's Statute requires further interpretation by this Trial Chamber to specify the subject matter jurisdiction of this Tribunal. Namely, with respect to the last clause of Article 7, subsection 3, which refers to punishment of perpetrators of wrongful acts. So our motion is in the nature of a jurisdiction motion, a motion asking this Trial Chamber to construe the subject matter jurisdiction of the Tribunal, under Article 7, subsection 3, to exclude the liability of a commander for the failure to punish a subordinate, where knowledge of a wrongful act by the subordinate is learned after the fact. Returning to Additional Protocol 1, the prosecution has cited Article 87 as another basis for failure to punish liability, but Article 87, which also appears on page 19 of the prosecutor's response, nowhere confers any liability of any sort on a commander. It refers exclusively to the parties, the high contracting parties, and what the parties will require a commander to do. It cannot be the basis of any liability for a commander, and is not. There is an extensive discussion in the briefs of whether any case law before prior to international tribunals involving war crimes can support a crime for failure to punish liability, standing alone. If the authorities cited by the prosecution are scrutinised -- and we do so in our reply brief -- this Trial Chamber will find that those cases do not support, they do not hold and stand for the proposition that failure to punish liability standing alone is an offence. They do also rely on certain military manuals, and I would like to say a word about that. First, we suggest that national military manuals certainly do not of and by themselves create international customary law. The prosecution cites, I believe, four manuals: the American manual, the British manual, the German manual and a manual of the SFRY. The German manual and the manual from the former Yugoslavia clearly do not support liability for failure to punish. The German manual, if one examines section 12.13, if I might have a moment. The German manual cited at the top of page 17 in the prosecutor's responsive brief simply talks about procedures to be followed when a superior learns about incidents and indicates that the superior shall clear up the facts and refer the matter. It does not create a specific offence or liability on the part of the commander, and it certainly does not create liability as a principal. There is a distinction, I must underscore, between conferring liability on a commander, as a principal. That is liability equivalent to the person who committed the wrongful act in question, based solely on the commander's failure to punish the subordinate having learned of the wrongful act after the fact. There is a difference between principal liability and liability for violating one's duty as a commander to carry out, to instigate appropriate disciplinary proceedings for subordinates, or otherwise discharge one's duties. The latter constitute matters of national law, disciplinary matters within military organisations, and that is clearly what section 12.13 of the German manual refers to. Also, if you look further down the page, on the prosecutor's response, at the manual from the former Yugoslavia, in section 21 we see the portion relied upon by the prosecution again for failure to punish liability. Here this section again draws the same distinction. In the first part of the section, it refers to a commander who does not charge subordinates responsible for an offence as being "personally responsible". It does not say that the commander shall have liability as a principal for failing to punish. It simply says they are personally responsible, which we submit means they are responsible as a commander for discharging the commander's duties, and a violation thereof is a matter of military discipline. Not international war crimes. If you turn, then, to the bottom of section 21, we see the other side of the coin, where the manual reads: "A military commander is responsible as a participant or an instigator if, by not taking measures against subordinates who violate the law of war, he allows his subordinate units and individuals to continue to commit the acts." That is failure to prevent liability, with which the defence does not argue. In other words, within section 21, the manual of the military, the former Yugoslavia draws the very distinction we are drawing. It does not in any way support liability based on failure to punish where the commander learns of the alleged crimes or offences after the fact. We also maintain that the very concept of liability for failure to punish where the commander learns of the alleged offence or crime after the fact of commission is, quite frankly, contrary to modern principles of international law in every system, and to illustrate that, I would like to describe something that I first found last night when reading the pre-trial brief of the Office of the Prosecutor in the Celebici case, a different case, and I am not citing it as necessarily the position of the prosecutor in this case, because I do not believe this specific issue will have application in this case. I am citing it by way of example, to illustrate the conflict between failure to punish liability as charged, and pursued by the Office of the Prosecutor, and fundamental notions of fairness, of individual culpability, personal guilt, causation, and so forth. In this trial brief, the Office of the Prosecutor in the other case I referred to argues, and I quote, that: "Under Article 7, subsection 3 of the Tribunal's Statute", and I am quoting from page 13, "the superior's duty to punish subordinates extends to violations that were committed before the superior was appointed, if he knew or should have known about these violations after he assumed command of the perpetrators, and in the event that the superior failed to take measures to punish the perpetrators in these circumstances." What the Office of the Prosecutor is saying in the other case in this trial brief is that, if a war crime was committed in 1991, and a commander was appointed, first arrived on the terrain two years later in 1993, if the commander should have learned about the war crime two years earlier, and failed to punish the perpetrators, that commander is liable as a principal, as an actor, as an instigator, as a perpetrator himself or herself of the underlying crime committed two years earlier. I think everyone in this courtroom must feel a pulling on their sense of ethical and moral fibres at that notion, that a commander could be held principally liable for something that was committed long before they arrived and took command, merely on the fact that they failed to punish a subordinate who had committed a crime at an earlier point in time, and we submit there is a reason why no Tribunal in history has punished failure to punish standing alone as an offence. With the court's permission, I would like to ask Mr Nobilo to briefly provide a perspective on this same issue from the perspective of the law of the former Yugoslavia. MR NOBILO (in interpretation): Mr President, your Honours, maybe what I am about to say is more linked to responsibility of commander, but it is also linked to failure to punish. So what I am going to say, please bear in mind what I am going to say now when discussing the following motion, after this one. The prosecutor's responsibility was based on the samurai justice, and the defence opposes this; the principle of an individual guilt. That is the basis of modern law, and of the legal system existing in Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the states in the former Yugoslavia. We define "guilt" as a subjective position of the perpetrator towards the act in the form of dolus malus and in the form of negligence. These are different degrees of guilt which differ in scope, and also in the extent of criminal liability, whereas for premeditated, this guilt is narrower, whereas in the case of negligence it is broader. Therefore, we feel that personal liability in the sense of Article 7, paragraph 3 of the Statute of this Tribunal should be defined as criminal liability in the form of premeditated offence, and therefore it can very clearly help us to define the liability of an individual. I shall present the reasons very briefly. A criminal act, a premeditated act is done by someone who is aware of that act and who wishes to commit it, or who was aware that a harmful act can ensue as a result, and, in the case of both forms of premeditation there is a common intellectual component, consciousness, awareness of the act, and there is a different wilful component. In one form he wishes the consequence, and in the other case, he agrees to it without wanting it. In the first, we call direct premeditation, and in the second, possible premeditation. Those are categories on which criminal law rests, but, regardless of which form of premeditation we have in mind, there must be awareness of the offence of the act. Whether that be proven by direct evidence or indications is less important. It is a factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr President, we are not getting a translation into English. (Short technical interruption) (5.00 pm) (A short break) (5.15 pm) JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): After this break, for reasons outside our control, I give the floor to Mr Nobilo. Do you hear me? MR NOBILO (in interpretation): Yes, I do, Mr President. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): You are going to resume from the moment when nobody can hear you any more. I cannot remember exactly when that was. Could you please show that you listened to the defence very carefully, so as to tell us when the sound stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, we lost our ability to hear Mr Nobilo perhaps for one minute. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): So you are going to resume from a point which will be understandable to everyone. On the other hand, I would like to ask you to speak more slowly, because for the booth, which does not have a text, such a fast translation is rather difficult. Thank you. You have the floor. MR NOBILO (in interpretation): Thank you. I checked on the computer screen, and I think I know up to what point the translation ran smoothly.
